turns.prompt_text: I need a terminal command so that I can take a folder full of images and chunk it into many subfolders with some number of images per each folder.
turns.response_html:
Here is a reliable terminal command to automatically organize your images into separate subfolders.

For Mac and Linux (Bash/Zsh)

Open your terminal, navigate to your folder containing the images using the cd command (e.g., cd /path/to/your/images), and then copy and paste the following command.

You can change the chunk_size=50 to however many images you want per folder.

chunk_size=50; i=0; for f in *.{jpg,jpeg,png,gif}; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; d="folder_$((i/chunk_size + 1))"; mkdir -p "$d"; mv "$f" "$d/"; ((i++)); done

How it works:

  • chunk_size=50: Defines the maximum number of files per subfolder.
  • for f in *.{jpg,jpeg,png,gif}: Finds all common image files in the current directory. (If you have other formats like .webp, you can add them inside the curly brackets).
  • d="folder_$((i/chunk_size + 1))": Calculates the correct folder number using division. It will create names like folder_1, folder_2, etc.
  • mkdir -p "$d": Creates the subfolder if it doesn't already exist.
  • mv "$f" "$d/": Moves the image into the designated subfolder.

For Windows (PowerShell)

If you are using Windows, open PowerShell, navigate to your image directory, and use this command instead:

$chunkSize = 50; $i = 0; Get-ChildItem -File -Include *.jpg,*.jpeg,*.png,*.gif | ForEach-Object { $dir = "folder_$([math]::Floor($i/$chunkSize) + 1)"; if (!(Test-Path $dir)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir | Out-Null }; Move-Item $_.FullName -Destination $dir; $i++ }

How it works:

  • Get-ChildItem -File -Include ...: Grabs all the specified image files in your current directory.
  • [math]::Floor($i/$chunkSize) + 1: Does the math to figure out which folder number the current image belongs in.
  • Test-Path & New-Item: Checks if the numbered folder exists, and creates it if it doesn't.
  • Move-Item: Relocates the file.

Would you like me to adjust either of these commands to handle specific file types, or to sort the images by their creation date before organizing them?

turns.prompt_text: All righty, so I'm running fish on a Mac terminal. Can we make these as human-readable as possible?
turns.response_html:
Ah, fish is a great choice! One of its best features is how cleanly it handles multi-line commands, which makes creating a human-readable script much easier.

Instead of a cramped one-liner, you can copy and paste this entire block directly into your fish terminal. It uses clear variable names, standard math functions, and comments to explain exactly what is happening at each step.

# 1. Set how many images you want in each subfolder
set files_per_folder 50

# 2. Start a counter at 0
set counter 0

# 3. Loop through all common image files in the current directory
for file in *.{jpg,jpeg,png,gif}
    
    # Safety check: skip if the file doesn't actually exist 
    # (prevents errors if a certain file type is missing)
    if not test -f "$file"
        continue
    end

    # 4. Calculate the target folder number (1, 2, 3, etc.)
    set folder_num (math -s0 "$counter / $files_per_folder + 1")
    set folder_name "folder_$folder_num"

    # 5. Create the folder if it doesn't exist yet
    mkdir -p "$folder_name"

    # 6. Move the image into the new folder
    mv "$file" "$folder_name/"

    # 7. Increase the counter by 1 for the next image
    set counter (math "$counter + 1")
    
end

How to use it:

  1. Open your terminal and navigate to your folder of images.
  2. If you want a different number of files per folder, just change the 50 in the very first line before copying.
  3. Copy the whole block above and paste it directly into your fish prompt. Press Enter, and it will run the whole loop.

Would you like me to show you how to save this as a permanent fish function so you can just type something like chunk_images 50 anytime you need it in the future?
